title: Love God, Serve Man -- Ch. 3: 'Salamat Po'
primary_topics: Chapter 3 of 'Love God, Serve Man' -- CJP's address at the Manila Hotel launching the RCM Eyebank Foundation, given almost entirely as a public thanksgiving to the benefactors, donor clubs and volunteer surgeons who made the country's only eye bank possible.

An accounting of the support raised: President Fidel V. Ramos' double Paul Harris contribution of P50,000, a $50,000 grant from the Foundation of Rotary International secured over two years, donations from five Asian sister clubs, local peso contributions and Canadian laboratory equipment, totalling P2,735,800 and expected to reach P3 million after the fining session.

The plea that makes up the second half: the Eyebank needs money, volunteer ophthalmologist-surgeons and, third, donors of eye tissue -- so he asks the audience to fill out donor forms and stages a raising of hands to enlist them.

The Eyebank placed in the Rotary Club of Manila's line of charitable institutions and tied to President Ramos' Philippines 2000 programme, with a pledge to reduce the incidence of curable blindness by at least 30 percent by the year 2000.
sub_topics: He speaks on behalf of the Foundation and of all the blind people who will soon see the color, movement and wonders of the world, thanking President Fidel V. Ramos for gracing the launching and for dedicating his double Paul Harris contribution of P50,000 to the Eyebank.

He thanks the Foundation of Rotary International for its $50,000 grant, made possible by two years of effort by former RI President Mat Caparas and former RI Director Benny Santos, and the sister clubs of Tokyo South, Kowloon East, Taipei, Taipei Central and Taipei Fu-Jung, along with the Paul Harris fellows and local donors listed in the Balita.

He thanks Rotarian Andre Simard, Canadian ambassador to the Philippines, for laboratory equipment given by the Canadian government, and reports total contributions of P2,735,800, which the finemaster Santi Dumlao's fining session is expected to round up to a neat P3 million -- enough for the Eyebank to be operationalized.

He thanks the volunteer Rotarian eye doctors and surgeons led by Dr. Ed Caparas and his son Dr. Victor Caparas, with Dr. Benny Santos, Dr. Jack Bautista, Dr. Rado Banzon and Dr. Carling Sevilla -- well-known ophthalmologists with full practices who cut down their leisure time to serve the poor.

He situates the Eyebank in the Rotary Club of Manila's 74-year record of founding humanitarian institutions -- the Philippine Tuberculosis Society, the Philippine Cancer Society, the Community Chest, the Boy Scouts of the Philippines, the Medico-Surgical Missions and Sagip Kabataan -- calling it the only facility of its kind in the country and possibly in Asean.

He explains the Eyebank's purpose and its three requirements: to collect and preserve eye tissue, particularly corneas, for implantation in the blind or near blind, which needs equipment, trained volunteer surgeons, and donors of tissue effective after death.
He makes the donor appeal personal and eternal: even when you are gone from this life, someone will always cherish you and pray for you because you made it possible for him to see the light of day.

He explains, self-deprecatingly, why a man who is neither philanthropist nor surgeon was made president of the Foundation, then calls for a raising of hands -- asking those NOT willing to donate to stand -- and, finding none standing, takes the whole Fiesta Pavilion as volunteers.

He closes by aligning the Eyebank with President Ramos' Philippines 2000 vision of a newly industrializing country fighting poverty, inequity and injustice, pledging to cut curable blindness by at least 30 percent by the year 2000 and repeating MARAMING, MARAMING SALAMAT PO.

notable_anecdotes: The finemaster's arithmetic: with P2,735,800 already in hand, past president Santi Dumlao, the dreaded finemaster of the day, promised that the fining session minutes away would round the total up to a neat P3 million -- and CJP says salamat po in advance to Monsignor Santi and all his hapless victims.

The self-deprecating explanation: he suspects the doctors on the board elected him president because, being neither a rich philanthropist who could donate equipment nor a surgeon who could implant tissue but only a poor but talkative lawyer, he could produce the one thing left -- donors.
The raising of hands: he asks all who are NOT willing to donate their eyes to stand up, finds that there are none, and takes everyone who stayed glued to their seats as a volunteer donor.

The surgeons who gave up their leisure: he notes that the volunteer ophthalmologists have enough patients to keep them busy all day all week, yet in the name of Rotary have cut down their leisure time to serve the poor, and asks the audience to applaud them.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 3 of 'Love God, Serve Man' is the address CJP delivered at the Manila Hotel launching the RCM Eyebank Foundation, and it is first of all a thanksgiving. Speaking on behalf of the Foundation and of all the blind people who will soon see the color, movement and wonders of the world, he thanks President Fidel V. Ramos for gracing the launching and dedicating his double Paul Harris contribution of P50,000 to the Eyebank; the Foundation of Rotary International for a $50,000 grant secured over two years by former RI President Mat Caparas and former RI Director Benny Santos; the sister clubs of Tokyo South, Kowloon East, Taipei, Taipei Central and Taipei Fu-Jung; the Paul Harris fellows and local donors listed in the Balita; and Rotarian Andre Simard, the Canadian ambassador, for laboratory equipment from his government. Contributions stood at P2,735,800, which the dreaded finemaster Santi Dumlao was expected to round up to a neat P3 million within the hour, enough for the Eyebank to be operationalized. He thanks the volunteer Rotarian ophthalmologists led by Dr. Ed Caparas and his son Victor, who have full practices yet cut down their leisure time to serve the poor. He then places the Eyebank in the Rotary Club of Manila's 74-year line of institutions, alongside the Philippine Tuberculosis Society, the Philippine Cancer Society, the Community Chest, the Boy Scouts and Sagip Kabataan, calling it the only facility of its kind in the country and possibly in Asean, and explains that it was set up to concretize the biblical gift of sight in our technological age by collecting and preserving corneas for implantation. Of the three things it needs -- equipment, surgeons and tissue donors -- only the third remains, and since he is neither philanthropist nor surgeon but only a poor but talkative lawyer, he supplies it by asking everyone to fill out donor forms, then calls for those unwilling to stand, finds none, and claims the whole hall. He closes by pledging, in keeping with President Ramos' Philippines 2000, to reduce curable blindness by at least 30 percent by the year 2000.
